```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(janitor)
```

```{r}
happiness_ranking <- read_csv("WHR26_2021.2.csv")
clean_names(happiness_ranking)
```
```{r}
social_spending <- read_csv("social_spending_2021.csv")
clean_names(social_spending)
```



```{r}
combined_data <- happiness_ranking |> inner_join(social_spending, join_by(`Country Name` == `Country Name`))
```

11/24 assignment tests:

```{r}
social_spending |> summarize (
mean_social_spending = mean(`Social Spending as Percentage of GDP`),
median_social_spending = median(`Social Spending as Percentage of GDP`),
sd_social_spending = sd(`Social Spending as Percentage of GDP`)
)
```
The mean and median are very close, which means that the data should not be extremely skewed and is somewhat symmetrical. 

```{r}
social_spending |> 
  ggplot() + 
  geom_histogram(aes(x = `Social Spending as Percentage of GDP`), binwidth = 2.5)+
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = mean(`Social Spending as Percentage of GDP`)), color = "red", linetype = "dashed", size = 1)+
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = mean(`Social Spending as Percentage of GDP`) - sd(`Social Spending as Percentage of GDP`)), color = "blue", linetype = "dashed", size = 1) +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = mean(`Social Spending as Percentage of GDP`) + sd(`Social Spending as Percentage of GDP`)), color = "blue", linetype = "dashed", size = 1)
  
```
This histogram shows that the data is pretty normally distributed. It is not perfect, but it generally follows a bell curve, and most of the data falls within 1 standard deviation of the mean. 



```{r}
combined_data |>
  ggplot(aes(x = `Social Spending as Percentage of GDP`, y = `Life evaluation (3-year average)`)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "red") +
  labs(x = "Social Spending as Percentage of GDP", y = "Happiness Score",
       title = "Countries' Happiness Score vs. Social Spending")
```
```{r}
model <- lm(`Life evaluation (3-year average)` ~ `Social Spending as Percentage of GDP`, data = combined_data)
summary(model)

happiness_model <- model
```
P-value: 0.006. This is statistically significant
Adjusted R-Squared: 15.27%. This means that the social spending percentage causes a 15.27% variation in a country's happiness score. This seems like there is an impact but it is not very significant. 
Coefficient: 0.04. This is positive which indicates that higher social spending leads to higher happiness scores. 0.04 is a very small coefficient, so the magnitude of this relationship is somewhat minimal.
